techniques.name: Breadth-first search
recognise: "Fewest steps", "shortest path" or "minimum number of moves" where every move costs the same.
A maze or grid with walls and a start and end point.
Also for "all cells reachable within N steps": BFS visits nodes in order of distance.

techniques.name: Dijkstra / weighted shortest path
recognise: "Lowest total risk / cost / heat loss" where moves cost different amounts.
Turning costs extra or movement rules depend on direction: make the direction part of the node.
If every move costs the same, plain BFS is simpler and faster.

techniques.name: Depth-first search & backtracking
recognise: "How many distinct paths" or "the longest route that never revisits a tile".
Longest path is hard in general: compress the graph to junctions first, then backtrack.
Building something piece by piece and undoing choices (bridges, schedules).

techniques.name: Search over puzzle states
recognise: The thing that moves is the whole configuration: elevators with items, amphipods in rooms, fights with mana.
Make the state a tuple or frozenset so it can go in a set, and BFS or Dijkstra over states.
Speed up by canonicalising equivalent states and pruning moves that are never useful.

techniques.name: Flood fill & connected groups
recognise: "Regions", "basins", "groups" or "clusters" of connected cells.
Area, perimeter or sides of each region (count edges facing a different region).
Connections arrive one by one ("connect the closest pairs"): union-find.

techniques.name: Topological sort
recognise: "Step C must be finished before step A can begin" or ordering rules between pages.
Reactions that need other reactions' outputs first.
Watch for the tie-break rule, often alphabetical.

techniques.name: Classic graph algorithms
recognise: Visit every point of interest in the best order: all-pairs distances first, then permutations (TSP).
"Largest set of computers all connected to each other": maximum clique.
"Cut three wires to split the graph in two": minimum cut (networkx has it if you install it).

techniques.name: Grid basics
recognise: Any 2D map of characters: parse it to a dict of (row, col) to char so bounds checks become "in grid".
Directions as a list of offsets and an index, so turning is index + 1.
Tilting or rotating the whole map: rotate the list of rows with zip.

techniques.name: Cellular automata
recognise: Every cell changes at the same time based on its neighbours (seats, octopuses, cubes, tiles).
Store only live cells in a set: works on infinite grids and in 3D or 4D unchanged.
"After a billion generations": combine with cycle detection.

techniques.name: Manhattan distance & directions
recognise: "Taxicab" or "Manhattan" distance, sensors with a range, wires crossing.
Turtle-style instructions (turn left, move forward): complex numbers make turning one multiplication.
A huge area with sensor diamonds: work per row with intervals, never cell by cell.

techniques.name: Hexagonal grids
recognise: Six directions like n, ne, se or e, se, sw.
Use cube coordinates: distance is the largest absolute coordinate difference.

techniques.name: Polygon area (shoelace & Pick)
recognise: "How many tiles are enclosed by the loop" or "how much lava does the lagoon hold".
Huge dig instructions where flood fill is too slow: shoelace area plus Pick's theorem.
Point-in-polygon for individual cells: count wall crossings along a ray.

techniques.name: 3D & geometry
recognise: Cubes, bricks or points in 3D: the grid tricks still work with 3-tuples.
"Exterior surface": flood fill the air around the shape instead of the shape itself.
Falling bricks or overlapping claims: sort by height or position first.

techniques.name: Modular arithmetic, LCM & CRT
recognise: Several independent loops must line up at the same moment: lcm of the loop lengths.
"Earliest timestamp where bus i departs i minutes after t": Chinese remainder theorem.
Numbers grow without bound but only divisibility matters: keep them modulo the product of the divisors.

techniques.name: Cycle detection
recognise: Part 2 asks for the state after 1,000,000,000 steps of a deterministic process.
Store each state with the step it appeared at; when one repeats, skip ahead by whole cycles.
Also "loops forever?" questions: a repeated (position, direction) state means a loop.

techniques.name: Linear equations
recognise: "Press button A and button B how many times": two equations, two unknowns.
Use Fractions for exact answers and check for whole numbers.
Hailstones or trajectories that must meet: set up the equations rather than simulating.

techniques.name: Divisors, primes & digits
recognise: "Elves deliver to every house that is a multiple of their number": sum of divisors.
A reverse-engineered program that counts non-primes or sums divisors.
Digit rules (never decreasing, splitting numbers in half) or unusual bases like SNAFU.

techniques.name: Differences & extrapolation
recognise: "Predict the next value" of a sequence: repeated differences until all zeros.
Growth that becomes quadratic over a repeating period: measure three points and extrapolate to the huge step count.

techniques.name: Permutations & combinations
recognise: Small number of items (about 10 or fewer) and "best order" or "best group": try them all with itertools.
"Every pair of points": combinations(points, 2).
Every choice of operator per gap: product(operators, repeat=n).

techniques.name: Memoization & dynamic programming
recognise: "How many ways" or "how many arrangements" with an answer far too big to enumerate.
A recursive function called with the same arguments over and over: add @cache.
Exponential growth where order does not matter (lanternfish, pebbles): count with a Counter.

techniques.name: Recursion & trees
recognise: Nested structure: lists within lists, packets within packets, monkeys yelling other monkeys' results.
Expression trees and custom operator precedence.
Very deep input: raise the recursion limit or switch to an explicit stack.

techniques.name: Binary search on the answer
recognise: "What is the first byte that blocks the path" or "the maximum fuel for 1 trillion ore".
Checking one candidate is easy and the answer flips from no to yes once.

techniques.name: Greedy choices
recognise: Pick the best option at each step and it provably never hurts later choices (largest digit first).
If a greedy answer is rejected, the puzzle probably needs DP or search instead.

techniques.name: Constraint elimination
recognise: Work out which field, opcode or allergen is which from a list of possibilities.
Some item always has exactly one option left: fix it and remove it everywhere else, repeat.

techniques.name: Intervals & range splitting
recognise: Ranges of IDs, seeds or coordinates in the billions: never expand them into numbers.
"Fully contains" or "overlaps": compare start and end points.
Mapping whole ranges through rules: split each range into the moved part and the leftovers.

techniques.name: Prefix sums & sliding windows
recognise: Sums over many windows or rectangles: precompute prefix sums once.
"First position where the last N characters are all different".
Compare each window to the previous one instead of recomputing it.

techniques.name: Interpreters & virtual machines
recognise: A list of instructions with registers and jumps.
"What is the accumulator right before an instruction runs a second time": track visited pc values.
Keep the interpreter small and testable: one function per instruction or a match statement.

techniques.name: Reverse engineering programs
recognise: The interpreter works but would run for hours or years.
Find the hot loop, translate it to what it really computes and replace it.
Input programs that repeat the same block with different constants (ALU, Chronospatial).

techniques.name: Circular lists & linked lists
recognise: Marbles, cups or elves in a circle with a current position.
Millions of insertions or removals in the middle: deque.rotate or a dict of next pointers, never list.insert.

techniques.name: Stacks
recognise: Matching brackets or cancelling neighbouring pairs.
Crates moved between piles: a list per pile with append and pop.

techniques.name: Bit manipulation
recognise: Masks with X, 0 and 1, binary strings, or seat codes that are really binary numbers.
A set of keys or valves as part of a search state: store it as one int bitmask.

techniques.name: Hashing
recognise: MD5 of a secret plus a number: brute force with hashlib, cache hashes that are reused.
The puzzle defines its own hash: implement the steps exactly as written.

techniques.name: Parsing input
recognise: Numbers scattered in text: grab them all with one regex and unpack.
Blank-line separated sections: split on two newlines first.
Corrupted memory with valid instructions hidden inside: one regex with alternatives.
